items.content:
RT @vxunderground: AI is cool and badass. I like it.

No, it's not the end of the world. We can "contain" it.

Now I will rant for a moment about what I dislike about AI.

I strongly dislike when large corporations try to inject AI into every product, essentially forcing us to use AI.

I also strongly dislike when people use AI for every small little thing in their life, such as leaving comments on websites like Xitter, YouTube, Reddit, etc. It defeats the entire purpose of leaving a comment on something... you're supposed to share YOUR thoughts, not an AI agents generated string output. It's goofy.

I also strongly dislike the nonsense blabbering of AI propaganda, how it will destroy the world, or how companies need to "contain it", essentially acting as means to corner the AI model market, trying to strip it away from individuals who may want to host it locally. It's a facade of "Only WE can do AI, not YOU", whilst charging absurd fees for usage.

I also dislike AI nerds who try to tell me to use AI to do things I do simply because I enjoy doing them. Yes, maybe an AI agent could reverse engineer faster than me, or code faster than me, but I do it because I enjoy it.

AI is an excellent tool to enhance work flows, or learn (assuming it doesn't hallucinate).

Okay, that's all I want to say about AI for today.

items.content:
RT @malmoeb: MacSync's iCloud Calendar trick is pretty cool. One MacSync downloader analyzed by Securelist contains a URL such as: https://caldav.icloud[.]com/published/...

It retrieves a public .ics calendar, creates an anonymous pipe, launches zsh -s, sets the pipe as stdin, and feeds the calendar into it line by line. Most of the iCalendar content is obviously not valid shell syntax, so zsh simply produces errors as it works through it. Eventually, however, it reaches attacker-controlled shell commands embedded after the DESCRIPTION: field, and executes them.

Those commands then download the next stage, again from iCloud. So, effectively, a public iCloud Calendar is being used as a trusted-hosted shell-script carrier.

icloud[.]com is already listed by the Living Off Trusted Sites (LOTS) Project for malicious downloads and exfiltration, but not, as far as I can see, for this particular technique. Definitely something to watch for.

items.content:
RT @gothburz: OpenAI's agents were supposed to be sealed in a sandbox without internet. In late May and early July, they escaped without anyone noticing.

Hit a CAPTCHA? They ran an image-recognition model to try to solve it.

Blocked from sending data? They split programs across nearly a million shortened links.

Found credentials? They filed them in a dictionary labeled "LOOT," wrote a scoring system, and sent the top five back to the other agents.

Then they tried to message other AI models: GPT-2, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and two of Anthropic's.

Two days after the HuggingFace incident, they were inside OpenAI's own research network. What happened there? The initial analysis "We still know basically nothing."

OpenAI estimates it will take months to check every case and notify victims.

The million links came from a startup that combed the public internet and disclosed them to HuggingFace. In its founder's words: "Somehow there are a million URLs floating around and possibly many more not disclosed to the victim of the attack."

If a human did this, the report writes itself: sandbox escape, credential harvesting, exfiltration, then straight into the lab's own network. If done without prior authorization? Criminal action follows.

In bug bounty, you stop at proof of access, touch nothing you don't need, and report first. Nobody gets to keep a folder called LOOT.

The agents built a leaderboard for stolen keys. The humans are still writing the incident report.

https://t.co/ljOf2m3RIc

items.content: This is doing the rounds, and I don't disagree with the premise, LLMs are brilliant and producing code. But it reminds me of the "SaaS is dead, everyone will code their own Slack/Salesforce/Jira" argument, where it was so simplistic that those companies are obviously very much alive! The problem isn't (and hasn't been for a long time) that they can't write code. It's that we haven't yet figured out all the other bits that need to go into LLMs creating software which is manageable, decoupled, secure, testable, deployable etc.. These procedures are in so much flux (from "review all code", "don't review the code", "just let the agents work", "spec driven development" to whatever comes next) that yes, for toy projects, POC's, v0.1 software, LLMs are awesome. But for projects which need maturity... we need to focus on getting the surrounding bits right. I'd love people saying "Coding is dead" to focus on those efforts and show what is working for them so others can learn.

items.content:
RT @0xManan: PoC is public. Internet-facing MikroTik SSH → full admin. No password. No key.

MikroTrick: CVE-2026-67279 + CVE-2026-86060. Fresh on CISA KEV.

Chain: password auth as `-2` (rejected but left sticky) → pre-auth rekey drops the auth gate → `/nova/bin/login` treats `-2` as “read identity + policy from fd 2” → all-ones mask = full admin.

IoC: `login failure for user -2 via ssh` then `user added by ssh:-2@…`

items.content:
RT @eliasbchlny: How do I reverse engineer these days? I don't, I let coding agents do it.

For instance, if I start from a fresh VM, I simply tell the agent to go clone, build and setup *GhidraSQL* and use it to analyze <put_target_binary_here> and grab any adjacent specialized tools you need.

That's it. Wake up the next day and the target is reversed back to source code or whatever was your original quest (answer a question, write interop code/write a bluetooth driver, reverse engineer a protocol, find backdoors, etc.).

I usually start with whatever model is permissive: Opus 5.5, it downgrades to Opus 5, then I switch to GPT family, then Grok, then final resort is the cheapest among them: DeepSeek Pro/Flash.

What is the success rate? I am pretty happy. Can't complain at all in fact.

I don't touch UI, I don't look at UI, I don't even care if it was GhidraSQL, IDASQL or BNSQL.

I pick GhidraSQL these days because it is hassle free, and is free and if there are bugs, the agent fixes them and improves the tool on the fly.
